body:
I can understand wanting to deduplicate end user actions, but it seems a bit less expected to deduplicate API calls and such as well. Maybe it's okay.

I also don't think we have the cookies (or many headers) available as part of the navigation algorithm currently. Fetch ends up adding those.

This proposal assumes a static network topology.  At risk of opening an even bigger can of worms, wouldn't it be better to race the two requests in case the second request finds a faster path through the network?  Imagine a case where the user navigates on poor cell data, then 1 second later successfully reconnects to good wifi, then 1 second later reclicks the same navigation.

FYI we have a draft spec [PR](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11765) now, let us know if we're missing anything. I think we need to add a way to [inform the navigation API about the aborted navigation][(https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/nav-history-apis.html#inform-the-navigation-api-about-aborting-navigation) without it being owned by the navigable yet, but I'll ask about it in the PR later.

> I can understand wanting to deduplicate end user actions, but it seems a bit less expected to deduplicate API calls and such as well. Maybe it's okay.

It is a little unexpected, but I'm not sure if there's an actual use case for triggering two practically identical navigation right after another outside of the user requesting it through e.g. double click on some button or something. If there are, I guess we can make carveout to specific cases (maybe just the `navigate()` API)?

> I also don't think we have the cookies (or many headers) available as part of the navigation algorithm currently. Fetch ends up adding those.

Oh interesting. Do you think we can just refer to the request's [header list](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-request-header-list) when comparing the navigations? At least the request's header list seems to be referred in [step 6.3 of "create navigation params by fetching" here](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsing-the-web.html#create-navigation-params-by-fetching)

> This proposal assumes a static network topology. At risk of opening an even bigger can of worms, wouldn't it be better to race the two requests in case the second request finds a faster path through the network? Imagine a case where the user navigates on poor cell data, then 1 second later successfully reconnects to good wifi, then 1 second later reclicks the same navigation.

Yeah it's definitely possible that a second navigation might actually get a response faster. However we've been experimenting and it looks like it's more common for this to help with latency overall. If we get really unlucky, the threshold is low enough (it's 1-3s in our impl) that another retry would actually trigger a new navigation. I guess we can make an exception to when the network actually changed, although I'm not sure how that looks like in spec. Any suggestions?
@rakina you can refer to it for sure, but at that point the header list is essentially empty, so I don't think it's useful, unless you mean to compare `Content-Type` specifically.

Oh that's a good point. Hmm, it looks like the [cookie header](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#ref-for-append-a-request-cookie-header) and other headers are added quite deep into the fetch algorithm, where it's probably hard to back out without disrupting things. So maybe instead we should compare specific properties that are important? Since we are restricting this to GET maybe we only need to check the cookies via [retrieve cookies](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-layered-cookies#name-retrieve-cookies) (and then compare it with the cookies in the header of the existing navigation). Will that be enough?

I think if you are really intent on comparing cookies you have to do the comparison in Fetch somehow, as it's conceptually (and practically in some implementations) a completely different layer. That seems rather involved however. But it also seems that comparing cookies would end up exposing some details, such as whether an HTTPOnly cookie was set since the initial navigation. Not sure that's information we'd want to give to an attacker.

Hmm, so maybe it's better to just not compare the cookies at all, with some risk of ignoring actually-different navigations? Is that acceptable, if the time limit is low enough? (Comparing only non-http cookies would be a bit incomplete for the purposes, and not sure if that's possible).

> Hmm, so maybe it's better to just not compare the cookies at all, with some risk of ignoring actually-different navigations? Is that acceptable, if the time limit is low enough? (Comparing only non-http cookies would be a bit incomplete for the purposes, and not sure if that's possible).

If this becomes an issue we could change this behavior based on whether the document itself changes anything that would affect the navigation after the first one (e.g. sets cookies).

> If this becomes an issue we could change this behavior based on whether the document itself changes anything that would affect the navigation after the first one (e.g. sets cookies).

Oh that's a good idea. Can we just make a wrapper for setting the [cookie attribute](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/dom.html#dom-document-cookie) and make that set a "last cookie update timestamp" or something and then only ignore if the last modification time is less than the original navigation's start time? Are there other API calls that can trigger cookie modifications etc to cover outside of that?

> > If this becomes an issue we could change this behavior based on whether the document itself changes anything that would affect the navigation after the first one (e.g. sets cookies).
> 
> Oh that's a good idea. Can we just make a wrapper for setting the [cookie attribute](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/dom.html#dom-document-cookie) and make that set a "last cookie update timestamp" or something and then only ignore if the last modification time is less than the original navigation's start time? Are there other API calls that can trigger cookie modifications etc to cover outside of that?

I think it can be a boolean "navigation conditions potentially changed" or some such, associated with the navigation when it starts and initialized at `false`, and becomes `true` if any API that *might* affect those conditions is called. If it's true, a second navigation can abort the first one; We can be pretty generous about setting it to true.
There's also the Cookie Store API, but any fetch that happens between the navigations can in theory impact the cookies.

What timeout did you use? It might be a source of interop issues if browsers have different timeouts.

I first thought it could maybe be the same as the "double click" timeout (which is already used for the `dblclick` event), but https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11743#issuecomment-3377560810 discusses clicking again 2 seconds later.

> What timeout did you use? It might be a source of interop issues if browsers have different timeouts.

I first thought it could maybe be the same as the "double click" timeout (which is already used for the dblclick event), but https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11743#issuecomment-3377560810 discusses clicking again 2 seconds later.

We experimented with 1s, 2s, and 3s, and are leaning to choose 3s since it has the best results in reducing latency. Going more than that seems risky and the increase in coverage isn't really significant. Looks like the `dblclick` threshold is [300ms](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:ui/events/gesture_detection/gesture_detector.h;l=44;drc=62a9a00176f862e688fa47919ed6f19b59f77b5f) in Chrome, I don't think we want to go that low.

> I think it can be a boolean "navigation conditions potentially changed" or some such, associated with the navigation when it starts and initialized at false, and becomes true if any API that might affect those conditions is called. If it's true, a second navigation can abort the first one; We can be pretty generous about setting it to true.

Sure, this sounds good to me. Do you have other things in mind that can set this outside of the many ways to change cookies?

> There's also the Cookie Store API, but any fetch that happens between the navigations can in theory impact the cookies.

Do we only need to care about `Set-Cookie` responses for the fetches? Is it reasonable to make those (and the Cookie Store API updates) update the bit above? (maybe excluding the HttpOnly ones?)

> However we've been experimenting and it looks like it's more common for this to help with latency overall.

Can you explain a bit more about the nature of the experiment(s)?

> Can you explain a bit more about the nature of the experiment(s)?

We tried enabling this on some population of Chrome, and measured metrics recorded by a partner site. Overall, they saw some decrease in navigations that they mark as exact duplicates, and a more significant reduction in the number of server responses that was sent but potentially never got shown/rendered in the browser (to detect "rendering", they send a beacon during load). This also improves their overall latency.  The metrics improvement increased as we increased the threshold (1s < 2s < 3s)

> This also improves their overall latency.

I don't quite understand this. How was this measured?

Also, was this across desktop and mobile?

They measure the time between when the user initiates the navigation (I think using the navigation timing API? But not sure) to when they've loaded enough content into their site (they have their own threshold on when that is). The latency savings is not huge, but maybe it's a side effect of not wasting capacity/network bandwidth maybe (not sure). They believe the user-perceived latency savings (which they don't have a way to measure yet) is likely more significant, since previously the user would've "wasted" the first X seconds for a navigation that eventually got cancelled.

We see the gains on desktop and mobile, but it seems to be higher on mobile. I guess mobile users have more tendency to click more often?

It _might_ be problematic that click event and such would still occur on an `<a>` multiple times, and thus also event listeners would get called multiple times, but the final steps of activation behavior only once. At least it would add some inconsistency to the platform (and inconsistencies tend to cause problems later).
If we were to make the ignoring explicit / web-observable, will that be OK? (not sure what the best way to surface that will be.. maybe somewhere in the navigation API)
FWIW, I was discussing about this with someone, and they were wondering if this is often an UI issue. Browsers aren't always super clear on whether navigation has started.

That's probably a factor, but at least in Chrome there's a pretty visible progress bar on mobile, and yet the duplicates seem more prevalent on mobile. If there are concerns on the ignoring being a surprise, I think there are two ways around this:
- Surface this through a new `navigationignored` event, which will be a `NavigateEvent`. Maybe the page can even do preventDefault to "un-ignore" the navigation (although I don't really see the use..)
- Make this an opt-in somehow. This is a bit tricky but maybe we can have a URL param that indicates this so that any duplicate nav containing that param is marked as safe to ignore? Or make an API on navigator that opts-in so that any duplicate navs triggered from that page can be safely ignored? The former would be more target-site-controlled and can cover navigations to that site coming from other sites, which will give more coverage here, so that's a bit nicer, but I'm not sure if it's possible to standardize that at all

Does any of those sound like a reasonable path forward here?

Thought of another way to look at this, with potentially a slightly modified version: instead of the navigation completely getting ignored, we can also just "throttle" the duplicate navigation, up until a specified time limit. If the original navigation actually committed within the specified time limit, the throttled navigation is dropped. If not, the new navigation is unthrottled and replaces the original navigation. That kind of captures the spirit of what we want to do here, which is not wasting work if it is still reasonable to wait.

Also, in practice, there's really never any guarantee that the second/duplicate navigation would actually replace the original navigation anyways. The navigation (at least in Chrome) goes from the renderer process through the browser process, and once it reaches a certain point, it becomes practically un-cancellable. Depending on how long it takes for the first navigation to get a response, and how long it takes for the second navigation to be processed in the browser process, it might be too late. Then when the first navigation commits, that would cancel the second navigation, or at least the outcome of the second navigation is just not visible to the initiator document (and the committed document is practically identical to what the second navigation would've committed anyways?)

An alternative way to think about this is that we don't ignore anything, we process both navigations fully except, if the request would be the same, the implementation is free to reuse the existing network request started by nav1 for nav2 instead of creating a new one. We don't need to tell the initiating document about this, so we have no new event and no need to worry about leaking httponly-cookie info.

Where the above has a problem is that performance timing info would weird. The navigation would look faster than it really was. So to avoid that, we should also move the timing info from nav1 to nav2.

Making this a network optimization might be conceptually simpler.

> Do you have other things in mind that can set this outside of the many ways to change cookies?

Referrer policy changes would be one thing. I guess this would only be triggerable via [`<meta name=referrer>`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/meta/name/referrer)? But the cookies thing is more concerning to me. @annevk is right in pointing out two things:

> any fetch that happens between the navigations can in theory impact the cookies.

This seems hard to integrate with a "reset" boolean that HTML would track in the navigation algorithm. I'm assuming Chromium doesn't do it like that? This brings me to:

> I think if you are really intent on comparing cookies you have to do the comparison in Fetch somehow, as it's conceptually (and practically in some implementations) a completely different layer.

IIRC, in Chromium all the cookie management is indeed at a different, lower "layer". So how does the Chromium implementation achieve cookie comparison? Does it do it at the "Fetch" level (basically deeper in to the Network Service, beyond `//content` navigation code)? If that's how most browsers would implement it and, then I think it's reasonable to push the major spec changes to that level in the spec too.

> I guess we can make an exception to when the network actually changed, although I'm not sure how that looks like in spec. Any suggestions?

I think it's ok for the spec to say UAs MAY skip deduplication if they known the network configuration has materially changed. Depending on the OS, the UA, and the nature of the change, they may not know this. A mobile UA would have a good chance to know that it was previously on cellular and has connected to wifi though.

(In other words, you don't have to define what constitutes a relevant network configuration change or make detecting one mandatory, in my opinion.)

We discussed this proposal in TPAC last month (see [slides](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/16pEyrIBy2N1I9wf6aawoBlRaIUDKV7AIPWPD-4YPP5o/edit?usp=sharing) and [minutes](https://www.w3.org/2025/11/11-whatwg-minutes.html)). I think we ended up converging on the initial version of this proposal (option 1 in the slides): the first navigation is kept, and the second navigation is dropped. The web-observable behavior should then be consistent with what happens:
- The `NavigationTiming` timestamps of the committed navigation (the first navigation) should reflect the first navigation. 
- We trigger events indicating that the second navigation is dropped, e.g. WebDriver cancel event.

On the criteria for duplicate navigation, it seems like the current list of condition in the initial proposal is ok, with some question on how to spec the cookie check exactly (I think @domfarolino offered to help figure this one out?). There was also some discussion on putting the exact time threshold in the spec. We're gathering some more data from the Chromium side and will report back on this. In the meantime, we'll work on refining the rest of the [spec PR](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11765) and start asking for reviews soon. Let us know if there are any remaining concerns!

> with some question on how to spec the cookie check exactly (I think @domfarolino offered to help figure this one out?)

My exact recommendation can probably be found in the TPAC minutes, but from memory I think it was basically: based on the fact that Chromium has a cookie change listener that exists well outside the network layer that surfaces network layer information to the navigation stack, we can basically just directly query the cookie store [kind of like fetch does](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#ref-for-name-retrieve-cookies), and say we expect implementations to implement this more gracefully, with some kind of authoritative listener mechanism that surfaces cookie-layer information up to when this decision is being made at navigation time. I'm hopeful that won't be too controversial.

An update on this: We're continuing seeing positive results from experimentation in Chrome and are looking into standardizing soon. One finding we found during implementation is the cookie change check discussed [previously](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11743#issuecomment-3380500423) should only be checking cookies that the initiator document itself changed, and not any other changes. This means it won't factor in HTTP-only cookie changes, and cookie changes triggered by other documents.

This is because dropping a navigation is inherently observable to the initiator document (e.g. through load event timing differences, and maybe other ways to observe via other web platform APIs). Adding checks for general cookie change state (that include all cookie changes) will leak whether any cookie change occurred between the two navigations (including same-origin HttpOnly and cross-origin cookie changes). So to avoid leaking any new information, we should only check information that is already known by the initiator document.

Also, due to complexities in implementation and also specification, I think we would want to exclude fetch-triggered cookie changes. Any fetch can update the cookies too, but because they're asynchronous and needs to go to the network service, so I'm not sure if there's any guarantee at all that these fetches will update the cookie before the second navigation hits the browser process. We believe users should not expect cookie updates from these fetches to take effect before the next navigation 100% of the time (especially because our max start time diff threshold is just 3s), even if it's triggered from the same document that initiates the navigations.

With all that, I think we would only have to consider cookie changes to `document.cookie` and CookieStore API that are triggered by the navigation initiator document. I think this is what was [proposed](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11743#issuecomment-3380515974) by @noamr earlier too. @llannasatoll is going to update the spec draft we have to account for these.

I think this is a terrible idea.

> We observe users sometimes navigate to the same URL in quick succession, likely by accident.

I **can't imagine a scenario** where I'd navigate multiple times to the same URL in quick succession **without it being on purpose**. I mean I _can_ imagine it happening but it would be _extremely_ rare.

"We observe"? Who is we? Where did you observe that? How? Did you observe repeated incoming requests on your servers? What is the basis for assuming that it happens "likely" by accident?

As a user, if I click a second time on a link because the first attempt is stuck or for whatever other reason, I would absolutely despise the browser **silently ignoring my explicit action** and doing nothing. I would be filled with rage.

I think [this comment](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11743#issuecomment-3377560810) is the perfect example of why this is completely insane.

Can anybody provide examples of scenarios where a second (or multiple additional) navigation(s) to a given url happens by accident??

A different thing is detecting an accidental double-click meant to be a click, but that's a completely different thing (we are talking hundredths of a second, not seconds) and it's basically a non-issue, because the first navigation is aborted so quickly that the wasted time and resources will almost always be negligible.
